I am seventy years old now, and though my knees ache when the weather turns, my hands still remember every ridge of this 10.1 mu. I have farmed it for twenty years, since I was fifty, and before that I watched my father do the same. My household has four people — my wife, my son, and my daughter-in-law — and they help me in the fields when the factory does not need them. We have our own well, so when the heavens forget to rain I can pump water, but diesel is dear and I am not young enough to haul pipes around for no good reason.

For wheat, I sow in early October. I use **improved seed** from the county supply station — not the old traditional kinds, but the hardy varieties they recommend. After the maize stalks are chopped, I do **rotary tillage** to ready the seedbed. I put down compound fertilizer as a base before sowing, then top-dress nitrogen twice: once when the wheat greens up in spring, and again at jointing. I will **irrigate three times**: the overwinter water in November so the seedlings do not freeze, the jointing water in March, and one more at grain-filling if May is dry. **Two pesticide sprays** are enough — a herbicide in early spring, and a second only if I see aphids or rust. This land has always been honest with me; if the weather holds, it will give **500 kilograms per mu**.

For maize, there is no time to dawdle after wheat harvest in early June. I use **no-tillage direct seeding** with **hybrid** corn seed — the single-cross hybrids the dealer sells. It saves my back and gets the crop in before the summer heat settles. I fertilize at sowing and side-dress more nitrogen when the plants reach the big-flush stage. **Two irrigations** will do: one right after sowing if the soil is dry, and the crucial one at tasseling in late July. **Two pesticide applications** — a herbicide at the 3-leaf stage, and one for corn borer if the moths appear. I expect **600 kilograms per mu**, maybe a little less if the rains come wrong.
